stem.text: The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = 5 \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 2 < c < 8 \), such that \( f'(c) = 1 \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(8) - f(2)}{8 - 2} = 1 \), f is not differentiable at \( x = 5 \), which lies in \( (2, 8) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[2, 8\right] \) is \( \frac{f(8) - f(2)}{8 - 2} = \frac{12 - 6}{6} = 1 \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[2, 8\right] \) and differentiable on \( (2, 8) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = 5 \), which lies in \( (2, 8) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = 1 \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(8) - f(2)}{8 - 2} = 1 \), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be continuous on \( \left[2, 8\right] \).
